title: Coppersmith's method for small divisors in a residue class of 4Cp+1
connection: Coppersmith/Howgrave-Graham: given N and a residue class r mod M with M ≥ N^{1/4}, one can find all divisors of N ≡ r mod M in polynomial time. ES needs a divisor of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C; here M = 4C and N ≈ 4Cp, so M ≈ N/p — far above N^{1/4} when C ≥ p^{1/3}.
why: This means the search for a Type-II-style certificate at fixed C is *algorithmically trivial* (lattice reduction) for large C — which says the hard part is purely existential, not computational, and makes the 'divisor in a class' lattice explicit (a 2-dim lattice whose short vectors are the certificates).
first_step: Write the Howgrave-Graham lattice for 'divisor of N in class r mod M' with N = 4Cp+1, M = 4C; identify the short vectors with (f, f′) of the Type II form; check whether the lattice's determinant structure explains the log²p count.

title: Factoring with hints (Rivest–Shamir, Maurer): ES as 'one divisor with 1/2 of the bits known'
connection: If a divisor f of 4Cp+1 is ≡ −1 mod 4C, then its low bits (mod 4C) are known; Maurer/Rivest–Shamir show factoring with half the bits known is polynomial. Conversely the *existence* of such a 'half-known' divisor for some C is ES.
why: The crypto literature's reverse question — for which N do such hint-structured divisors exist for a given hint modulus — may have been studied for key-generation (e.g. 'RSA keys with prescribed residue primes').
first_step: Search 'divisors in a prescribed residue class existence density Lenstra' (Lenstra 1984, 'Divisors in residue classes'): Lenstra bounds the NUMBER of divisors in a class by a constant when M > N^{1/3}; check what this says about ES's counting shape (at most O(1) certificates per large C).
refs: H. W. Lenstra Jr., 'Divisors in residue classes', Math. Comp. 42 (1984)

title: Lenstra's 'divisors in residue classes' upper bound vs ES's needed lower bound
connection: Lenstra (1984) proves: the number of divisors of N in a fixed class mod M with M > N^{1/3} is ≤ 11 (and the divisors are computable). ES needs ≥ 1 for some C ∈ [1, ∞) with N = 4Cp+1, M = 4C.
why: Lenstra's proof is via a 2-D lattice and continued fractions — exactly the ES₅ CF-length structure; understanding why his argument caps the count might show what forces the count to be ≥ 1 somewhere (or that it cannot).
first_step: Read Lenstra 1984 §2; map his lattice to the Type II pair (f, f′); determine whether ES₅ (λ ≤ 3) is Lenstra's condition for a specific convergent.

title: Approximate-GCD problem (van Dijk–Gentry–Halevi–Vaikuntanathan) and the Type I form
connection: Type I: f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p mod 4cd. Many samples p² + 4c²d (varying c,d) each near a multiple of an unknown f is the 'approximate GCD' setting from homomorphic encryption; its hardness/easiness results describe when such common divisors exist.
why: AGCD theory has precise density statements for when noisy multiples share a divisor; flipping to existence is an ES-like 'tied' question.
first_step: Write the Type I condition as p² ≡ −4c²d (mod f): a quadratic residuosity condition (−d is a square mod f up to units). Compare with the AGCD lattice attack (Cohn–Heninger 2011) to see whether it enumerates ES certificates.

title: SAT/SMT encoding of ES for a symbolic prime: unsat core as a proof template
connection: Encode '4/p has no solution with x,y,z < p² and p ≡ 1 mod 24' with p as a bit-vector of width w; for each w the solver returns UNSAT (if ES holds there). The UNSAT cores / DRAT proofs for w = 8, 10, 12, … might converge to a human-readable argument.
why: Heule's SAT-based proofs (Pythagorean triples, Schur 5) found structure humans missed; the per-width proof sequence is a cheap experiment nobody seems to have run for ES.
first_step: Write a CNF via bit-blasting of 4xyz = p(xy+yz+zx) with x ≤ y ≤ z < 2^{2w}, p < 2^w; run kissat/cadical for w ≤ 12 with proof logging; inspect core size growth.

title: Presburger/automatic-sequence test: is the set of (p, C_min(p)) k-automatic in any base?
connection: Automatic sequences and k-regular sequences are decidable by Walnut; if the first winning C (or Type I minimal c) were k-regular in p, Walnut could *prove* ES in that regime. Almost certainly not, but the negative result would be informative: it shows ES is 'non-automatic' which rules out all finite-automaton covering proofs.
why: Cheap and decisive one way or the other; connects to B1 in automaton language.
first_step: Compute C_min(p) for p ≤ 10⁶, test for 2-/3-/10-regularity with a k-kernel rank test (compute subsequences C_min(k^e p + r) and check linear dependence).
refs: Shallit, 'The Logical Approach to Automatic Sequences' (Walnut)

title: Decidability frontier: ES as a Π₁ sentence of bounded-quantifier arithmetic — is it provable in IΔ₀ + exp?
connection: ES is Π₂ (∀n ∃x,y,z) but with the bound x,y,z ≤ n² (true for ES? solutions can be bounded by n² in Type II forms? check) it is Π₁ with bounded search. Reverse-mathematics / bounded-arithmetic questions: which fragment proves the known partial results (Mordell identities are in IΔ₀; Vaughan's sieve needs exp).
why: Proof-theoretic strength calibration tells what style of argument can possibly work: if ES is provable in IΔ₀+Ω₁ then there is a 'polynomial-size certificate' explanation, which constrains the proof shape.
first_step: Check whether there is always a solution with max(x,y,z) ≤ n² (compute for n ≤ 10⁵; known bounds for Type II give z ≤ ...). Then search 'Erdős–Straus bounded arithmetic' / 'unit fractions IΔ0'.

title: Kolmogorov complexity of the solution 'script' (c,d,f) across primes
connection: For each p, encode the lexicographically first Type I/II solution as a string; measure compressibility across consecutive primes (gzip of the concatenation, or a learned model's perplexity). Low complexity = hidden rule.
why: Direct test for 'there is a simple hidden rule the campaign has not found'. Cheap.
first_step: Produce the (c,d,f) first-solution sequence for p ≤ 10⁶, compress with xz/zpaq, compare with compressibility of a surrogate random sequence with the same marginals.

title: Program synthesis (enumerative/DreamCoder) for a 'solution formula' with branching on residues
connection: Search the space of programs 'if p ≡ r mod M then (x,y,z) = (polynomials in p)' with sqrt/floor allowed (non-polynomial! escaping Mordell–Schinzel) that output a valid ES solution on as many primes as possible.
why: Mordell–Schinzel kills polynomial identities on square classes; identities with floor, gcd, or ⌊√p⌋ are not covered by that theorem and nobody has systematically searched them.
first_step: Define a DSL: polynomials in p, ⌊√p⌋, ⌊p/k⌋, gcd(p+a, b), residue branching; run enumerative search (depth ≤ 6) scoring on primes ≡ 1 mod 840 up to 10⁵; report best coverage.
refs: Mordell–Schinzel (no polynomial identity on square classes)

title: Symbolic regression on f(p) to find a closed-form main term with explicit arithmetic corrections
connection: Fit f(p) ≈ A log²p + B log p · g(p) + ... where g ranges over arithmetic features (number of prime factors of p−1, p+1, class number h(−p), h(−4p), least QNR, Legendre symbols of small primes).
why: If a class-number or L-value feature explains a large part of the variance, it hints that f(p) is 'really' a class-number-type quantity (which would be an exact-formula route).
first_step: Build a feature table for primes ≤ 10⁶ (h(−4p), h(−p), ω(p±1), (2/p),(3/p),(5/p),(7/p), smallest prime factor of 4p+1, 8p+1, 12p+1 …); run PySR/LASSO on f(p)/log²p; report R².

title: Gradient-boosted classifier for 'p has a solution with C ≤ 10' and inspect feature importances
connection: Train a classifier on arithmetic features of p to predict whether a small-C certificate exists; if accuracy is high, the features used ARE a partial identity; if accuracy ≈ base rate, small-C solvability is 'random' w.r.t. all tested features.
why: Cheap, directly reveals structure or its absence in the bounded-C regime (the covering regime).
first_step: Features: p mod 840·k, Legendre symbols of primes ≤ 50, ω and smallest factors of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 10; target: exists C ≤ 10 with a winning divisor. Train/test on p ≤ 10⁷.

title: Transformer trained on (p → first solution) to test for learnable 'algorithm'
connection: Train a small transformer on digit sequences p ↦ (x,y,z) for p ≤ 10⁶; test extrapolation to larger p. Charton-style experiments show some arithmetic tasks (GCD, modular arithmetic) are learnable with interpretable circuits.
why: If a model generalises beyond training range, mechanistic interpretability might extract an algorithm; if it cannot, that's weak evidence of no simple algorithm.
first_step: Replicate Charton's GCD-transformer setup with ES targets; measure out-of-range accuracy.
refs: Charton, 'Can transformers learn the greatest common divisor?' (2023)

title: Learned certificates: train a model to output C given p, verify by exact arithmetic (AlphaProof-style)
connection: The solution search is 'find C'; a learned prior on C (given features of p) could shrink the search and, more importantly, expose which C-values are 'predictable'.
why: A predictable C-function would be an identity candidate; non-predictability calibrates against covering-type proofs.
first_step: Train a regressor from p-features to log C_min(p); compare against baseline (median); inspect residuals vs p mod 840.

title: Hidden-shift/period structure in the e-slice subset-product sets
connection: The set S_N(e) = {ab⁻¹ mod e : ab | N} is a 'sumset' in log coordinates; Freiman/Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers structure theorems describe sets with small doubling, and the group-theoretic Kneser theorem gives |S + S| bounds. ES needs −1 ∈ S for some e.
why: Additive-combinatorics structure of S_N could show S_N(e) is 'almost a subgroup' for many e — then membership of −1 is a character-sum question.
first_step: Compute |S_N(e)| and |S·S| relative to e for p ≤ 10⁵ and all admissible e ≤ 4p; look for e where S is a near-subgroup.

title: Complexity-theoretic: is 'ES certificate search' in a class with natural proofs of totality (TFNP subclasses)?
connection: ES says the search problem 'given p, find (x,y,z)' is total. TFNP classes (PPA, PPP, PLS) each correspond to a combinatorial existence principle (parity, pigeonhole, local search). Which principle, if any, would ES's totality be an instance of?
why: PPA-totality = parity argument (e.g. Chevalley–Warning, Smith's theorem), PPP = pigeonhole (Minkowski). If ES is placed in PPA, a parity proof is the target; the campaign has parity-type observations (T1 is a sign) but no parity *proof*.
first_step: Try to express ES as 'a graph with an odd-degree vertex has another' (PPA): build a graph on near-solutions where degrees are determined locally; see if one known odd-degree vertex (e.g. the trivial 'degenerate' solution 4/n = 1/n + 1/n + 2/n?) forces another.

title: Chevalley–Warning / Ax–Katz over ℤ/p: count solutions of 4xyz ≡ n(xy+yz+zx) mod primes to force integer ones
connection: Chevalley–Warning gives p | #solutions mod p of low-degree systems in many variables; the ES equation mod a prime q ≠ p has q² + O(q) points. Can a divisibility invariant on the *integer* solution count (like Markoff's orbit sizes ≡ 0 mod p) be derived?
why: Chen's Markoff proof used an orbit-size divisibility; an analogue 'f(n) ≡ something mod m' with a nonzero RHS would be a parity-type proof of f(n) ≥ 1.
first_step: Compute f(n) mod 2,3,4,6 for n ≤ 10⁵ and check for any forced congruence (e.g. is f(p) always odd for p ≡ 1 mod 24?). Note symmetry: solutions come in permutation orbits, so count orbits.

title: Combinatorial Nullstellensatz for the ES polynomial on a product set
connection: Alon's CN: a polynomial of degree Σ d_i with nonzero coefficient on Π x_i^{d_i} has a non-root on any product set S_1×S_2×S_3 with |S_i| > d_i. ES wants a *root* of 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) in a product set — the dual question, but CN-type 'non-vanishing then counting' arguments (e.g. for Cauchy–Davenport) sometimes yield existence of roots of auxiliary polynomials.
why: Listed in the repo's deep-lane catalogue; the free-lane twist: apply CN to an auxiliary polynomial whose non-vanishing implies an ES root (e.g. Π over candidate (x,y) of (something)).
first_step: Try: fix n, consider F(x,y) = Π_{z ∈ Z}(4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx)) over a set Z; CN gives a non-root of F in product sets, i.e. (x,y) such that no z ∈ Z works — the wrong direction. Try instead the polynomial method over F_q with q | some 4Cp+1.

title: Proof-assistant mining: formalise the Type I/II divisor equivalence in Lean/mathlib
connection: mathlib has Egyptian fraction basics? (check: `Nat.Egyptian`? probably not). Formalising the reduction ES(p) ⟺ divisor condition would be a modest contribution and forces every hidden assumption into the open.
why: Formalisation has repeatedly exposed gaps and suggested generalisations; also a public Lean statement attracts collaborators.
first_step: Search mathlib for 'egyptian' and 'unit fraction'; search GitHub for 'Erdős–Straus Lean'; draft the statement `∀ p, Prime p → p % 4 = 1 → (∃ x y z, 4*x*y*z = p*(x*y+y*z+z*x)) ↔ ∃ c d f, ...`.

title: Mine the Lean 'Erdős problems' formalisation project for ES-adjacent lemmas
connection: Erdős problems site + Lean formalisation efforts (e.g. Erdős #306 nearly formalised). ES is Erdős problem #… (check the erdosproblems.com number) — see what lemma infrastructure exists for unit-fraction problems there.
why: Infrastructure reuse; cheap.
first_step: Visit https://www.erdosproblems.com and search 'Straus'; check the associated GitHub for Lean files.

title: Reverse-engineer Salez's 10¹⁷ verification code for implicit structure (which identity family covers which prime)
connection: Salez's verification used a specific set of identities/searches; the *distribution of which family fired first* across primes up to 10¹⁷ is data nobody has analysed for structure.
why: A 'which rule saved this prime' census is a cheap large-scale pattern-discovery dataset.
first_step: Locate Salez's paper/code (arXiv 1406.6307 'The Erdős–Straus conjecture: new modular equations and checking up to N=10^17'); re-run the family census for p ≤ 10⁹ and tabulate first-firing family vs p mod 840.

title: Gröbner basis / elimination for the system {Type I condition, Type II condition} as polynomial equations with p symbolic
connection: The Type I/II parametrisations are polynomial identities in (c,d,f,p). Elimination ideals over ℤ[p] could expose hidden relations between simultaneous Type I and Type II solutions of the same p.
why: Relations between the two types (e.g. a Type I solution implies a Type II for a related prime) would be a new 'persistence' tool.
first_step: In Singular/Macaulay2, set up the ideal generated by 4xyz − p(xy+yz+zx) with x = pA, etc., and compute elimination ideals; look for any surprise generator.

title: Knuth–Bendix / term rewriting view of the 'Egyptian fraction identities' and confluence
connection: The family of identities (e.g. 1/n = 1/(n+1) + 1/(n(n+1))) forms a rewriting system on multisets of unit fractions; ES asks whether 4/n rewrites to a 3-element multiset. Confluence/termination theory could classify reachable lengths.
why: Formal rewriting makes 'what can be derived from splitting identities' a decidable question in restricted cases; the known tiny families (Bleicher–Erdős) would fit.
first_step: Define rewriting rules: split 1/a → 1/(a+1) + 1/(a(a+1)), merge 1/a + 1/b → 1/c when possible; compute reachable 3-term representations from the greedy 4-term one for n ≤ 1000.

title: Ramsey-type unavoidable patterns: among any K consecutive primes ≡ 1 mod 24, must one have a solution with C ≤ 2?
connection: Even if not every prime has a small-C solution, maybe 'small-C solvability' has bounded gaps along primes (van der Waerden-ish). Not ES itself but a sub-statement with a combinatorial flavour.
why: Bounded-gap statements can be proved by covering + pigeonhole; data shows which K is plausible.
first_step: Compute the longest run of consecutive primes ≡ 1 mod 24 up to 10⁸ with no C ≤ 2 (resp. ≤ 5, ≤ 10) solution.

title: Streaming/sketching: minimal information about p needed to construct a solution
connection: Communication-complexity framing: Alice knows p mod M, Bob knows ⌊p/M⌋; how much communication is needed to agree on an ES solution? If O(1) bits suffice for some M, that's a covering system; if Θ(log p), solutions are 'global'.
why: A clean quantitative version of 'ES is not local' (Mordell–Schinzel says polynomial-local fails; this asks for any protocol).
first_step: Empirically: for M = 840, compute for each residue class r the size of the smallest 'dictionary' of solution templates (c,d) needed to cover all primes ≡ r up to 10⁶; growth with the range.

title: Hash-function / pseudorandomness: treat (p ↦ prime factorisation of 4Cp+1) as a PRG and ES as 'PRG never outputs the all-miss pattern'
connection: Cryptographic pseudorandomness would *predict* P(miss) ≈ exp(−c log²p) and that misses happen for some p; ES asserts that they never happen — i.e. the map is detectably non-pseudorandom in the lower tail.
why: Forces a clear statement: either ES's 'never' is a coincidence of the small-count regime (and there IS a counterexample), or there is a structural correlation across C. The question 'which' is the campaign's central dilemma; the crypto framing suggests testing *higher-order correlations* across C.
first_step: Measure pairwise and triple correlations between the events 'C wins' and 'C′ wins' for p ≤ 10⁷; compare to independent model.

title: LLL on the 3-variable ES equation directly: find small solutions to 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) = 0 via Coppersmith bivariate
connection: After fixing x (≈ n/4 + small), the equation in (y,z) is a bivariate integer polynomial of bidegree (1,1): (4x − n)yz − nx(y+z) = 0 ⇒ ((4x−n)y − nx)((4x−n)z − nx) = n²x². So solutions are divisor pairs of n²x² in classes — Coppersmith's bivariate method finds small roots.
why: The factorisation ((4x−n)y − nx)((4x−n)z − nx) = n²x² is the classical two-term reduction; the 'small root' regime y,z ≤ n^{1+ε} may be exactly where solutions live. Quantify.
first_step: Check numerically: for p ≤ 10⁶, what is min over solutions of max(y,z)/p? Does a solution with max ≤ p^{3/2} always exist? (Relates to known bounds on denominators.)

title: Smallest-solution growth: is min_{solutions} max(x,y,z) ≤ p^{1+o(1)}?
connection: Bounds on the size of the smallest solution are a different pointwise statement than existence; the exponent governs which algorithmic approaches (Coppersmith bivariate: roots up to N^{1/3}…) could be made *provably* complete.
why: If the smallest solution has max coordinate ≈ p^{3/2} typically, then no 'small roots' method is complete; if ≈ p log p, there's hope for a lattice-based constructive proof.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁷ the smallest max-coordinate solution and fit the growth exponent; check repo for existing data (git grep -i 'smallest solution\|max(x,y,z)').

title: Word problem in SL₂(ℤ): ES as membership of a specific matrix in a product of three 'elementary' cosets
connection: Repo mentions SL₂ words. Membership-in-product-set problems in SL₂(ℤ) are decidable (automaticity of SL₂) and have automaton-theoretic structure; the 'length ≤ 3' condition of ES₅ is a bounded word length.
why: Automata for SL₂(ℤ) (via the free product ℤ/4 * ℤ/6) give a regular-language description of 'length ≤ 3 words'; the question becomes whether a regular language intersects a p-dependent set, which is sometimes handled by Büchi-type decidability over (ℕ, +, V_k).
first_step: Write the ES₅ word form as an explicit matrix product with entries depending on p; check whether the condition is 'matrix M_p is in L' for a regular L in the generator alphabet.

title: Constraint-propagation / arc-consistency on the (c,d,f) space to prove 'no solution' is contradictory
connection: CSP solvers find contradictions by propagating constraints; for a *symbolic* p (represented by its residues mod many small moduli), propagation might derive that 'no solution for any C ≤ K' contradicts p being prime ≡ 1 mod 24 for some K.
why: This is the covering-system search re-done with a general-purpose propagator that can also use quadratic-residuosity constraints (not just congruences) — which Mordell–Schinzel does not forbid.
first_step: Encode: p ≡ r mod 840; for each C ≤ K, all divisors of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C forbidden ⟹ constraints on Legendre symbols (−C/q) for q | 4Cp+1; propagate; look for contradiction with K ≤ 20.

title: Pseudo-Boolean / ILP relaxation: lower bound f(p) via LP duality on the e-slice counting polytope
connection: Write f(p) = Σ over e-slices of #{(a,b)}; an LP relaxation with constraints from divisor-sum identities (Σ_e over slices of total divisor counts = known) might give a dual certificate f(p) ≥ 1 if the identities are strong enough.
why: LP duality turns 'existence' into 'an explicit positive combination of known identities exceeds 0' — a proof template that is mechanically checkable.
first_step: Set up for p = 1009 (small): variables = indicator of each (e, a, b) candidate; constraints = all linear identities the campaign knows (divisor totals per e, M_BM-type sums); solve the LP; see whether the LP bound is > 0.

title: Sum-of-squares (Positivstellensatz) certificate that the ES count is positive for a symbolic p in a residue class
connection: Positivstellensatz gives algebraic certificates of positivity of polynomials on semialgebraic sets; the ES count isn't polynomial in p, but a surrogate (e.g. a weighted divisor sum with explicit character expansion) could be expressed via finite sums over residues of p mod M.
why: SOS has proved inequalities in combinatorics (flag algebras) that were beyond human reach; the challenge is finding a finite algebraic surrogate.
first_step: Fix M = 840; express Σ_{C ≤ K} Σ_{d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 (4C)} 1 ≥ (Σ over C of a quadratic-character sum in p mod stuff) and see if any lower bound depends only on p mod M.

title: Boolean function analysis: Fourier spectrum of the indicator 'C wins for p' as a function of p mod 4C·something
connection: For fixed C, whether 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C depends on p via the factorisation of 4Cp+1; its Fourier spectrum over p mod M (M a multiple of 4C) measures 'junta-ness'.
why: A low-degree Fourier concentration for all C would be a covering-ish structure; spectrum spread across high frequencies says the event is genuinely 'global'.
first_step: Compute, for C ≤ 20 and M = lcm(4C, 840), the Fourier spectrum (over ℤ/M) of E_p[win_C(p) | p ≡ r mod M] for p ≤ 10⁷.

title: Property testing: can one certify ES(p) with o(log p) queries to an oracle for the factorisation of 4Cp+1?
connection: Query complexity of the existence problem given a factorisation oracle: how many C must be queried in the worst case (empirically) before a winner is found? The query sequence design (adaptive vs non-adaptive) is the algorithmic skeleton of a proof.
why: Worst-case query counts over p ≤ 10⁸ calibrate the 'depth' of a proof (K queries ⇒ a K-case argument).
first_step: Record C_min(p) distribution (non-adaptive) and design an adaptive rule (choose next C based on factorisation of previous 4Cp+1); measure the max number of queries for p ≤ 10⁷.

title: Automated theorem proving on the 'two-term' lemma with a free parameter: Vampire/E on the divisor form
connection: First-order provers can sometimes prove number-theoretic lemmas given axioms about divisibility; the lemma 'if p ≡ 1 mod 24 and p < 2^k then ∃C ≤ K ...' is a bounded statement they might handle for small k.
why: Low chance, but the prover's search traces for small k might reveal which lemmas are reused — a proof-skeleton extraction.
first_step: Encode the divisor form in TPTP with Peano arithmetic axioms + bounded quantifiers; try Vampire for k ≤ 8.

title: Zero-knowledge-style 'succinct witness' for ES(p): what is the shortest certificate as a function of p?
connection: A solution (x,y,z) is a 3·log p-bit witness; a (C, divisor) is 2·log p bits; the ES₅ CF form is ~log p + small. The minimal witness length (information-theoretically) across p is a 'compressibility of the certificate'.
why: If a witness of O(log log p) extra bits beyond p exists for every p (i.e. 'which of polylog many templates'), ES is 'almost covered' by a polylog-size list — a different proof shape than existing ones.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10⁷, the minimal index of a winning C in the ordering by C; its log is the witness length; compare growth with log log p.

title: Union-find / disjoint-set structure of 'solution sharing' between different primes
connection: Two primes share a template if the same (c,d) with the forced f gives solutions for both. Build the graph on primes ≤ X with edges = shared template; connected components and their growth describe how 'global' the solution structure is.
why: Giant-component formation would indicate a Markoff-like 'strong approximation' phenomenon; many tiny components would indicate per-prime independence.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, list templates (c,d) of all solutions, build the bipartite prime–template graph, compute component structure.

title: Monte-Carlo tree search over 'proof strategies' for small residue classes (AlphaZero for covering systems)
connection: The search for a covering system of identities is itself a game tree; MCTS/RL has found covering-type constructions in other settings (e.g. Wagner's RL for combinatorial counterexamples). Target: maximal density of primes ≡ 1 mod 840 coverable by degree-≤2 identities with moduli ≤ M.
why: Not a proof, but establishes the best achievable 'partial cover' and whether the uncovered set has structure (squares + ?).
first_step: Reproduce the known cover (Mordell + Salez families) as a baseline; implement the RL search over identity templates; report uncovered density vs M.
refs: Wagner, 'Constructions in combinatorics via neural networks' (2021)

title: Quantum annealing formulation of ES as QUBO — purely to inspect the energy landscape
connection: Encode the bit-blasted equation as a QUBO; the spectrum of the Ising Hamiltonian (gap between ground state and first excited) across p measures 'hardness'; a gap that scales mildly suggests structure.
why: Cheap curiosity test; may reveal p-dependence of the landscape.
first_step: Build QUBO for p ≤ 200 via standard multiplication gadgets; exact-diagonalise small instances; plot gap vs p.

title: Compressed sensing / sparse recovery: f(p) as a sparse combination of character sums
connection: Express f(p) (or its Type I part) as Σ_χ c_χ χ(p) over characters of various moduli (it's not periodic, but truncated versions are); sparse recovery finds the dominant characters. Dominant terms = the identities that matter most.
why: Quantifies 'how periodic is f(p)' beyond Mordell's mod 840; a sparse spectrum would suggest a near-covering.
first_step: Fit f(p) − A log²p on p ≤ 10⁷ against characters mod M ≤ 10⁴ with LASSO; list top characters.

title: Model-checking a finite abstraction: ES for p 'with all small primes' residues fixed' as a finite transition system
connection: Abstract p by its residues mod all primes ≤ B and by its Legendre symbols; a finite-state system over these abstractions can be model-checked for the property 'some C ≤ K yields a divisor in class'. Counterexample traces are candidate hard residue profiles.
why: Finds the exact abstract profile of a potential counterexample; such profiles could then be hunted at 10¹⁸ (adversarial search guidance).
first_step: Enumerate profiles of p mod 840 and Legendre symbols (q/p) for q ≤ 31; for each profile, compute the empirical fraction of primes with C_min ≤ 10; find worst profiles.

title: Error-correcting codes: solution sets as codewords, and ES as 'minimum distance ≥ 1 from the zero word'
connection: Define for each p the binary vector v_p ∈ {0,1}^K with v_p[C] = 1 if C wins. ES(p) for C ≤ K ⟺ v_p ≠ 0. The set {v_p} is a 'code'; its minimum weight (over p) and its dual structure may reveal linear constraints among the C's.
why: Linear constraints among win-events (over F₂) would be exactly the parity invariants that could force a win.
first_step: Compute v_p for K = 64 and p ≤ 10⁶; compute the F₂-rank of the matrix and look for low-weight dual codewords (parity checks).

title: Database cross-reference: OEIS sequences around f(n), C_min, and Egyptian-fraction lengths
connection: OEIS has A073101 (number of solutions of 4/n), A192787, etc. Looking at the 'sequences that reference these' and their formulas/comments may reveal a connection the campaign missed.
why: Cheap and occasionally very fruitful.
first_step: Fetch OEIS A073101, A192787, A192788, A192789 and all sequences citing 'Erdős–Straus'; read comments and formulas; list any with unexpected cross-references (e.g. to class numbers, Bernoulli, Markoff).

title: Grover-style amplitude amplification is irrelevant, but the quantum query lower bound technique (adversary method) applies to classical 'how many C must be tried'
connection: Adversary bounds give lower bounds on queries needed to find a winning C against a worst-case p; translated classically: any proof that tries C in a fixed order needs ≥ max C_min(p) cases.
why: Makes precise that a 'list of templates' proof must have unbounded length — reinforcing Mordell–Schinzel from an algorithmic angle, but also showing adaptive proofs are not bound by it.
first_step: Just note it; verify unboundedness of C_min(p) numerically (if C_min were bounded a finite cover would exist — contradiction with Mordell–Schinzel only for polynomial covers; so unbounded C_min is a separate empirical question!). Compute max C_min(p) for p ≤ 10⁸.

title: Is C_min(p) actually bounded? (sanity question separating covering from identities)
connection: Mordell–Schinzel forbids *polynomial* identities on square classes but does not forbid 'for every prime p ≡ 1 mod 24 some C ≤ 10⁶ works'. If C_min is empirically bounded (e.g. ≤ 1000 up to 10¹⁸) that is a striking structural fact; if it grows like log p, there is no finite cover at all.
why: This is the single most basic calibration of the 'covering' approach and the question is sharp and cheap.
first_step: git grep -il 'C_min\|bounded C\|smallest C' -- '*.md'; if absent, compute max_{p ≤ 10⁸} C_min(p) with C in Type II form and in e-slice form.

title: Lattice attack on 'ES with x fixed to the greedy choice': when does greedy-first-term lead to a two-term remainder?
connection: The Fibonacci–Sylvester greedy picks x = ⌈n/4⌉; the remainder (4x−n)/(nx) with 4x − n ∈ {1,2,3} is a two-term sum iff a divisor condition on nx holds. For 4x − n = 1: 1/(nx) is one unit fraction, so greedy gives 2 terms? No: n ≡ 3 mod 4 case gives 1/(nx) — that's the easy class. For n ≡ 1 mod 4, 4x − n = 3 and 3/(nx) must split into two unit fractions.
why: The hard class p ≡ 1 mod 4 is exactly 'is 3/(p·⌈p/4⌉) a sum of two unit fractions, or else choose a non-greedy x'; the two-term criterion for 3/m is classical (3/m = 1/a + 1/b iff m has a divisor pattern mod 3). Making the 'non-greedy x' choice explicit is the whole game and the lattice view (x free, divisor of p²x² in class) is clean.
first_step: Tabulate for p ≤ 10⁶ the smallest x ≥ ⌈p/4⌉ such that (4x−p)/(px) is a two-term Egyptian fraction; study x − ⌈p/4⌉ distribution (is it O(log p)? polylog?).

title: Bit-level pattern mining on winning C in binary (are winning C's 'smooth'? 'prime'? 'powers of 2'?)
connection: The multiplicative structure of winning C matters (4C is the modulus); test whether winning C are biased toward smooth numbers, primes, or specific residue classes mod 3, 5, 7.
why: A bias (e.g. winning C is often a multiple of 3 for p ≡ 1 mod 3) is a candidate identity direction; cheap.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶ collect all winning C ≤ 1000; compare their distribution of ω(C), smoothness, C mod 12 against the uniform baseline.

title: De Bruijn / universal cycle: does a single 'universal' residue sequence of C's cover all primes up to X with O(log X) entries?
connection: Hitting-set problem: find the smallest set S of C's such that every prime p ≤ X has a winner in S. Its growth |S(X)| in X (constant? log X? X^ε?) is the 'covering dimension' of ES.
why: If |S(X)| = O(log X) with a nice structure (e.g. S = {1,2,3,6,...} products of small primes), a 'nested cover' proof shape emerges.
first_step: Greedy set-cover on the prime–C incidence matrix for p ≤ 10⁷, C ≤ 10⁴; report |S| vs X.

title: Tropical geometry of the ES surface: the tropical variety of 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) and lattice points on its 'tentacles'
connection: Tropicalising the cubic surface gives a piecewise-linear complex whose lattice points approximate valuations of solutions; the 'size' of solutions (val_q(x), …) lives on the tropical surface.
why: Tropical methods count/locate solutions by valuations — maybe they explain the preferred shape (one coordinate ≈ p, others ≈ p²/…).
first_step: Compute the tropical hypersurface of the Newton polytope of 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) (with n's valuation as a parameter) and plot where known solutions' (log x, log y, log z) fall.

title: Reed–Solomon-type interpolation: can the map p ↦ (x,y,z) be interpolated by a low-degree polynomial over a finite field F_q?
connection: Over F_q (q a prime of size ~ range), the 'first solution' map restricted to primes is a function; its degree as a polynomial over F_q (via interpolation) compared to the number of points measures 'algebraicity'.
why: If the map had degree far below the number of points for structured subsets (e.g. primes in a fixed class mod M), those subsets are covered by an algebraic rule — a new identity family.
first_step: Take primes ≡ 1 mod 840 up to 10⁵, interpolate C_min(p) mod q as a polynomial in p mod q, check the degree vs number of points; expect full degree (no structure) — a negative result calibrates B1.

title: Verification scale-up as a lead generator: GPU search for primes with anomalously small f(p)
connection: Adversarial search beyond 10¹⁸ for 'hardest primes' (minimum f(p)/log²p) over structured families (p with many small QNRs, p = m² + small); the hardest ones are the stress tests for any candidate mechanism.
why: Repo has adversarial data; extending it with GPU and a better hardness oracle (Legendre-symbol profiles) is cheap and gives a test suite for proposed proofs.
first_step: Define a hardness proxy from Legendre symbols (p/q) for q ≤ 50 (minimising predicted small-C wins); sample 10⁶ primes near 10²⁰ with worst proxy; count solutions on C ≤ 10⁴.
